title: From Production Chemistry to Interfacial Reactions: Low- and Moderate-Temperature Biochar and Hydrochar for Integrated Wastewater Treatment
authors: B. Kayan and A. Alver · Reactions
abstract: This critical review examines the potential of low- and moderate-temperature biochar and hydrochar for wastewater treatment, emphasizing the relationship between production conditions, surface chemistry, and contaminant removal. Particular attention is given to materials produced at temperatures up to 250°C and their comparison with higher-temperature derivatives. The review highlights the roles of surface functional groups, mineral interactions, and organic domains in removing metals and organic pollutants. It also evaluates the effects of feedstock characteristics, water chemistry, material modification, and regeneration on treatment performance. Key challenges include long-term stability, sorbent reuse, and limited engineering-scale evidence. The study emphasizes the need for reliable performance, cost, and environmental assessments before practical implementation.

title: Palladium nanoparticles supported on biochar/graphitic carbon nitride as a heterogeneous catalyst for pharmaceutical degradation
authors: P. Yekan Motlagh et al., including B. Kayan · Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering
abstract: This study investigates a palladium nanoparticle-supported biochar/graphitic carbon nitride (Pd@BC/g-C3N4) nanocomposite as a heterogeneous sonocatalyst for removing pharmaceutical pollutants from wastewater. Under optimized conditions, the catalyst achieved 94.23% tetracycline degradation within 120 minutes, outperforming the unmodified BC/g-C3N4 material (78.33%). The enhanced performance was associated with the uniform distribution of palladium nanoparticles and the generation of hydroxyl radicals during ultrasound treatment. Reusability experiments demonstrated good catalytic stability, while analysis of degradation intermediates indicated substantial transformation of tetracycline toward smaller organic compounds. These findings highlight the potential of palladium-based biochar composites for advanced wastewater treatment and sustainable pharmaceutical pollutant removal.
